rationale: בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.3.1) opens both the row and the part, the first of the four verse-initial address slots repeated at 3.21, 4.10, and 4.20 (bni_address inventory: 17 tokens book-wide, four heading this part). Two imperative-plus-consequence couplets follow: retain the father's teaching for length of days (3.1-3.2), then bind kindness and truth on the heart for favor with God and man (3.3-3.4). The row closes at the petuchah after Prov.3.4 (oshb:Prov.3.4, single-witness); the couplets beginning at 3.5 each name אֶל (oshb:Prov.3.5) directly, while neither couplet in 3.1-3.4 does.
rejected_alternative: Extending the row through 3.12 was rejected because the couplets from 3.5 onward each name אֶל (oshb:Prov.3.5) directly, a naming shift the petuchah at 3.4 (oshb:Prov.3.4, single-witness) corroborates but does not itself drive.

device_notes: Synonymous parallelism binds each couplet's two half-lines -- teaching and commandments at web:Prov.3.1 “My son, don’t forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments,” and kindness and truth at 3.3; the neck-and-heart-tablet figure of 3.3 gives the abstract virtue pair a concrete, wearable image.

rationale: From 3.5 through 3.12 four imperative-plus-consequence couplets each name אֶל (oshb:Prov.3.5) -- trust (3.5-3.6), fear and turn from evil (3.7-3.8), honor with substance (3.9-3.10), and accept discipline (3.11-3.12) -- five אֶל tokens across the row's eight verses, a naming density that sets these couplets apart from the teaching-retention pair of 3.1-3.4, where the divine name never appears. The petuchah after Prov.3.10 (oshb:Prov.3.10, single-witness) falls inside the row, between the honor couplet and the discipline couplet, without ending it: both keep the same imperative-plus-consequence shape and both name אֶל, so the mark corroborates an internal pause rather than the row's own edge. The row ends before 3.13, where the address shifts from second-person imperative to a third-person beatitude formula.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the row at the petuchah after 3.10 (oshb:Prov.3.10, single-witness) was considered and set aside: the honor couplet before it and the discipline couplet after it keep the same construction and both name אֶל (oshb:Prov.3.5), so the mark falls inside one naming-density unit rather than at its edge.

row ends before the third-person beatitude formula opening 3.13
device_notes: Each couplet pairs synonymous halves (trust/lean at 3.5, fear/turn at 3.7); the fourth couplet (3.11-3.12) varies the pattern with a father-son simile rather than a bodily-benefit result, a texture shift within the shared construction.

rationale: The row opens with אַשְׁרֵ֣י (oshb:Prov.3.13) governing 'the man' in third person, a genre break from the second-person imperative address running since 3.1 -- the tier-1 signal opening the poem the strategy flags as a bounds-argue candidate. The praise of wisdom continues through 3.18, which closes with  (oshb:Prov.3.18), a participle sharing the same root as the opening אַשְׁרֵ֣י and forming a root-level inclusio around the personal-benefit half of the poem (more precious than jewels, length of days, riches, pleasant paths, a tree of life). The petuchah after Prov.3.18 (oshb:Prov.3.18, single-witness) falls at that inclusio's close. The couplet at 3.19-3.20 extends the poem from personal benefit to cosmic scope -- אֶל (oshb:Prov.3.5) founding the earth and establishing the heavens by wisdom and understanding -- before the row ends at the return to second-person address at 3.21.
rejected_alternative: Ending the row at 3.18, with the petuchah there (oshb:Prov.3.18, single-witness) as the boundary, was considered and set aside: 3.19-3.20 continue third-person wisdom-praise rather than opening a new address, so the mark reads as an internal inclusio-close rather than the poem's outer edge.

device_notes: Synonymous parallelism describes wisdom's value in 3.14-3.17 (profit/return, precious/incomparable, right hand/left hand, pleasantness/peace); 3.19-3.20 shifts to a synthetic pair (earth-founding building on heaven-establishing) rather than synonymous restatement, marking the poem's move from human benefit to cosmology.

rationale: בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.3.21) reopens second-person address at 3.21, the part's second lecture-opening slot (matching 3.1, 4.10, 4.20). The row keeps sound wisdom and discretion before the addressee's eyes as one extended promise: life and grace (3.21-3.22), secure walking and untroubled sleep (3.23-3.24), and freedom from sudden fear because אֶל (oshb:Prov.3.5) is the addressee's confidence (3.25-3.26). No petuchah or other disclosure-object note falls inside this span; the row ends before 3.27, where the object of each admonition shifts from the addressee's own wisdom-keeping to the addressee's neighbor.
rejected_alternative: A narrower cut after 3.24, separating the wisdom-admonition (3.21-3.24) from the fear-admonition (3.25-3.26), lacks any parashah or disclosure-object support, and both halves keep the same second-person, self-directed object, so the wider bound is kept instead.

device_notes: Synonymous parallelism (eyes/heart at 3.21 continuing into life/grace at 3.22, lying down/sleep at 3.24); only 1 of 3 admonition-plus-consequence movements in this row -- the closing one (3.25-3.26) -- names אֶל (oshb:Prov.3.5) explicitly as the ground of confidence, a slight intensification toward the row's close.

rationale: Five consecutive prohibition imperatives open at 3.27 and run through 3.31, each addressing conduct toward another party -- withholding good from its owner (3.27), delaying a neighbor's due (3.28), plotting against a neighbor (3.29), needless strife (3.30), and envy of a violent man (3.31) -- a list-register run distinguishing this unit from the self-directed wisdom-keeping of 3.21-3.26. Three of the five verses carry ketiv/qere notes (3.27, 3.28, 3.30) and 3.28 also carries a paseq, all single-witness disclosure objects internal to the row; none functions as a boundary driver. The row ends before 3.32, where a two-letter conjunction introduces a shift from second-person prohibition to third-person gnomic rationale.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the five-verse prohibition list into narrower pairs (for example 3.27-3.28 / 3.29-3.31) was considered and set aside: no parashah or disclosure object marks an interior boundary, and all five verses share one prohibition-imperative construction. Reading 3.27 as a tov-min ('better than') comparative is a mandated rival to disclose: 3.27 is itself a ketiv/qere verse (oshb:Prov.3.27, disclosed above), and its contiguous טוב מ skeleton pairs with a source-marked object ('withhold good from its owner') rather than the comparative construction shared by the sweep's three other hits, Prov.15.16, Prov.16.8, and Prov.16.16.

device_notes: The prohibition series varies its grammatical object across the five verses (owner, neighbor twice, opponent, violent man) while keeping the prohibition-imperative shape constant, a construction-run cohesion rather than a shared-theme cluster.

rationale: A two-letter conjunction (oshb:Prov.3.32) opens 3.32 and shifts the discourse from the second-person prohibition series of 3.27-3.31 to four third-person gnomic statements pairing אֶל (oshb:Prov.3.5)'s disposition with a human outcome: abomination versus friendship (3.32), curse versus blessing (3.33), mockery versus grace (3.34), and glory versus shame (3.35). The row closes at the petuchah after Prov.3.35 (oshb:Prov.3.35, single-witness), the last verse before chapter 4 opens with a plural address at 4.1.
rejected_alternative: Folding 3.32-3.35 into the same unit as 3.27-3.31 was set aside: the conjunction opening 3.32 (oshb:Prov.3.32) marks a discourse turn to rationale-giving, and the shift from second-person imperative to third-person gnomic statement is a construction change the shared 'conduct toward another' theme alone would not justify keeping together.

device_notes: Antithetic parallelism structures all four sayings (abomination/friendship, curse/blessing, mockery/grace, glory/shame), a texture distinct from the synonymous couplets of 3.1-3.26.

rationale: שִׁמְע֣וּ בָ֭נִים (oshb:Prov.4.1) ('listen, sons') opens chapter 4 with a plural address, distinct from the singular address term shared by 3 of 4 lecture-openers in this part (3.1, 3.21, 4.10, 4.20). The row sets up a father's instruction (4.1-4.2), then recounts his own childhood as an only son (4.3) before introducing his own father's reported words with וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לִ֗י (oshb:Prov.4.4) ('and he said to me') in 4.4, a speech-frame device that itself completes one admonition-plus-consequence couplet. The row ends there, before the quoted instruction's own imperative pair opens fresh at 4.5.
rejected_alternative: Keeping 4.1-4.9 as one unit was considered: nothing marks 4.4/4.5 with a parashah or disclosure object, so the seam rests on the speech-frame device alone (וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לִ֗י (oshb:Prov.4.4)) rather than corroborated tier-1-plus-tier-3 evidence, which is why this boundary is held at lower confidence rather than folded together.

device_notes: The mise-en-abyme structure (a father quoting his own father) is unique across 62 verses in this part; synonymous parallelism continues in 4.1-4.2 (listen/pay attention; instruction/understanding).

rationale: The quoted paternal instruction introduced at the close of 4.4 continues here with a fresh imperative pair, קְנֵ֣ה חָ֭כְמָה קְנֵ֣ה בִינָ֑ה (oshb:Prov.4.5) ('get wisdom, get understanding'), echoed again at the head of 4.7, an internal repetition bracketing 4.5-4.7 before the row closes with wisdom personified as a figure who exalts, honors, and crowns the one who embraces her (4.8-4.9). No disclosure object falls inside this span. The row ends before the part's third lecture-opener at 4.10.
rejected_alternative: Splitting 4.5-4.7 from the personification lines of 4.8-4.9 was considered and set aside: the repeated קְנֵ֣ה חָ֭כְמָה קְנֵ֣ה בִינָ֑ה (oshb:Prov.4.5) imperative and the result clauses that follow it read as one continuous appeal rather than two, so no interior seam is argued here.

device_notes: Synonymous parallelism throughout (get wisdom/get understanding at 4.5 and 4.7; exalt/honor and esteem/embrace at 4.8); the crown-and-garland image of 4.9 closes the quoted instruction with a concrete reward figure paralleling the neck-and-tablet figure of 3.3.

rationale: שְׁמַ֣ע בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.4.10) ('listen, my son') reopens the singular address at 4.10, the part's third bni-opening (after 3.1 and 3.21, before 4.20). The row moves from the father's promise of long life for heeding his sayings (4.10) through his own testimony of having taught the addressee wisdom's way (4.11) and its unhindered walking (4.12) to a closing admonition to hold instruction fast, 'for she is your life' (4.13). No parashah or other disclosure-object note falls inside. The row ends before 4.14, where the imperative's object shifts from 'instruction' (self-directed) to 'the path of the wicked' (other-directed avoidance).
rejected_alternative: A shorter cut after 4.11, isolating the teacher's own testimony from the walking-result clause of 4.12 and the hold-fast admonition of 4.13, would break a single unbroken second-person address that carries no internal mark to support a narrower span.

device_notes: The row moves from promise (4.10) through testimony (4.11) to result (4.12) to renewed admonition (4.13), a four-beat progression rather than a repeated couplet pattern, distinguishing its internal texture from the couplet-built rows of 3.1-3.26.

rationale: בְּאֹ֣רַח רְ֭שָׁעִים אַל תָּבֹ֑א (oshb:Prov.4.14) ('into the path of the wicked, do not enter') opens a prohibition pair against the wicked way (4.14-4.15), followed by a third-person rationale describing those who cannot sleep until they do evil and who feed on wickedness and violence (4.16-4.17; the ketiv/qere at Prov.4.16, oshb:Prov.4.16, sits within this rationale). The row closes with an antithetic couplet contrasting the righteous path with the wicked way (4.18-4.19), ending at the petuchah after Prov.4.19 (oshb:Prov.4.19, single-witness). The row's own object -- the path to avoid -- distinguishes it from the self-directed instruction-holding of 4.10-4.13.
rejected_alternative: Separating the prohibition pair (4.14-4.15) from its rationale and closing contrast (4.16-4.19) was considered: the four verses share one grammatical subject ('the wicked'/'they') running continuously from 4.16 through 4.19, so no interior tier-1 seam supports a narrower cut.

device_notes: Antithetic parallelism closes the row at 4.18-4.19 (light/darkness, growing brightness/stumbling blindness); web:Prov.4.18 “But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light that shines more and more until the perfect day.” pairs directly with web:Prov.4.19 “The way of the wicked is like darkness. They don’t know what they stumble over.”.

rationale: בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.4.20) reopens the singular address at 4.20, the part's fourth and final bni-opening. The row promises life and health for keeping the father's words before the eyes and within the heart (4.20-4.22), then narrows to a single-organ progression: the heart as life's wellspring (4.23), the mouth and lips (4.24), the eyes (4.25), and the feet and their path (4.26-4.27), closing both the chapter and the part. The row's own front seam, Prov.4.19, carries a petuchah (oshb:Prov.4.19, single-witness), external to 4.20-4.27.
rejected_alternative: Cutting the row after 4.22, separating the general attend-and-live admonition from the heart-mouth-eyes-feet progression of 4.23-4.27, was considered and set aside: that seam carries no disclosure-object support of its own, and the second-person addressee and imperative mood carry unbroken from 4.20 through 4.27.

device_notes: The organ-by-organ sequence is a list-like register texture, though not chunked as a numerical_saying since it lacks an x-of-y counting formula; נְצֹ֣ר לִבֶּ֑ךָ (oshb:Prov.4.23) ('keep/guard your heart') at web:Prov.4.23 “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” is the pivot phrase anchoring the whole progression.
